The station stood at the narrow throat of the peninsula, where the spruce trees gave way to slate-grey shingle and the Atlantic breathed against the pilings like a sleeping beast. In the official ledger of the Northern Maritime Railway, it was recorded only as Junction 14, though no junction had existed there for forty years. The second track had long since surrendered to coastal bramble, sea-thrift, and salt-rust, leaving a single ribbon of iron that appeared to begin in the pine shadows and end directly in the cold, foaming surf.

Miller did not mind the isolation. Isolation possessed a rhythm, not unlike the brass pendulum of the Seth Thomas clock mounted above the ticket window, swinging with a dry, mechanical certainty that outlived storms. Every morning at dawn, Miller trimmed the wicks of the platform lanterns, swept the floor with pine-scented sawdust, and boiled chicory coffee on the potbelly stove. The coffee tasted of scorched earth and chicory root, but it was hot, and in late November, heat was the only currency that truly mattered.

No trains were scheduled. That was the bureaucratic truth. If one consulted the timetable published in the provincial capital, Junction 14 was marked only with a small, discreet dagger indicating *Flag stop; daylight hours; conditional upon weather.* But trains came anyway. They were not spectral—Miller possessed an excessively practical mind and had no patience for folklore—they were simply late. Terribly, exquisitely late.

Some had departed inland depots thirty or forty years prior, delayed by forgotten washouts, strikes, snowdrifts in the mountain passes, or the slow, quiet disintegration of the towns they had been built to serve. When they finally rounded the granite bluff, their boilers wheezing and their headlamps throwing butter-colored beams through the salt mist, Miller would step onto the platform with his kerosene lantern, raise it three inches above his right shoulder, and bring the consist to a halt.

Tonight, the wind smelled of iodine, wet kelp, and incoming sleet. The Seth Thomas clock struck eight—eight brass clangs that vibrated through the spruce floorboards and died among the dry rafters.

Then, the iron sang.

It was a faint, resonant vibration at first, the low *G* of cold metal under immense compression. Miller took down his heavy wool overcoat from its iron peg, settled his peaked cap, and pulled on his stiff leather mittens. He stepped out onto the cedar planks of the platform just as the locomotive emerged from the pines.

It was an ancient 4-4-0 American type, its black enamel scoured to bare, oxidized iron by thousands of miles of weather. Steam curled from its cylinder cocks in billowing, fragrant clouds of tallow and wet coal smoke. It slowed without the shriek of modern air brakes, coming to rest with a heavy, sighing shudder that settled the ballast beneath the ties.

A single vestibule door on the third coach creaked open on dry hinges.

The passenger who stepped down was wearing a tailored overcoat cut in the fashion of a previous generation, though its charcoal wool was immaculate and dry. He carried no trunk, only a heavy folio envelope made of rag parchment, sealed with a coin of dark green wax. He did not look out at the grey expanse of the ocean, nor back toward the dark forest; he looked directly at Miller.

"Is this the water's edge?" the traveler asked. His voice sounded like dry gravel shifting beneath a receding tide.

"It is," Miller said. "The line terminates two hundred yards past the signal shack. Nothing beyond that but cold water and Greenland."

The traveler nodded slowly, as though verifying an old coordinate. "Then I am on time."

"You have a while before the return," Miller said, gesturing with his lantern toward the station door. "Fire’s banked. There’s coffee, if you have a stomach for chicory."

The traveler hesitated, then stepped into the amber square of light spilling from the waiting room. Inside, the warmth was immediate, rich with the smell of cedar wood and drying wool. The traveler did not sit on the varnished oak bench. Instead, he walked to the cast-iron stove, holding his bare hands near the radiating heat. His fingers were long and pale, the skin translucent as drafting paper.

"I carried this from the Ministry of Works," the traveler said, placing the green-sealed envelope upon the ticket counter. "I was instructed to bring it to the last manned post on the eastern grid."

"I’m the only one left on the board," Miller replied.

"I know. They told me that when I set out. They said: *Travel until the rails run into the tide, and leave it with whoever is tending the light.*"

Miller walked behind the grille and picked up the folio. There was no name inscribed upon the parchment, no postal stamp, only the embossed insignia of an anchor crossed with a surveyor’s compass—the emblem of an agency dissolved before Miller was even a boy.

"What is recorded here?" Miller asked.

"A census of things that did not arrive," the traveler said softly. "Shipments lost between junctions. Letters mailed from towns that changed their names overnight. Passengers who stepped onto platforms for a breath of air and were left behind in the dark. It was thought proper that someone keep the accounting."

Miller ran his thumb over the hard edge of the wax seal. "I keep the station log," he said. "That is the job."

"Then the ledger is yours."

The passenger turned and walked back to the doorway. He did not ask for food, nor did he linger to let the warmth penetrate his coat. Outside, the locomotive gave a single, pure blast of its whistle—a sound that swept out over the Atlantic, startling roosting terns from the cliffs.

The iron wheels found their grip without slipping. The coaches rattled past, their windows dark and curtained, until the red lantern on the observation platform disappeared into the fog, retreating back down the single track toward the continent.

Miller stood on the platform until the iron stopped vibrating, until the only sound left in the world was the rhythmic, indifferent wash of the surf against the shore.

He returned inside, latched the heavy spruce door against the rising gale, and sat at his roll-top desk beneath the clock. He uncorked his inkwell, dipped a steel-nibbed pen into the black ink, and opened the daily register.

*November 24,* he wrote in his steady, copperplate hand. *Wind out of the northeast, force six. One train arrived from the interior. One parcel received into custody. The lamps were trimmed and the lights kept burning. All is well.*

He set the pen in its groove, turned the lamp down to a low, golden ember, and sat listening to the pendulum divide the night into small, manageable pieces.
